claim: Neurons can maintain stable activity profiles over their lifetimes despite ion channel turnover over minutes to weeks.
source: Neurons can maintain stable activity profiles over their lifetimes despite ion channel turnover over minutes to weeks.
evidence: This is a general statement about neuronal stability that is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Neuronal activity is influenced by regulating the voltage dependence of ion channels.
source: Neuronal activity is also influenced by regulating the voltage dependence of ion channels.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The timescale of activity-dependent regulation mechanisms shapes the specific electrical activity patterns that achieve a target activity profile.
source: These findings reveal that the timescale of these mechanisms shapes the specific electrical activity patterns that achieve a target activity profile.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract, supported by the computational modeling results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Alterations in channel voltage dependence can impact a neuron's ability to recover from perturbations.
source: Moreover, alterations in channel voltage dependence can impact a neuron's ability to recover from perturbations.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the perturbation simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Neurons homeostatically regulate channel number to stabilize their activity.
source: Experimental studies have shown that neurons homeostatically regulate both channel number (Desai et al., 1999; Haedo and Golowasch, 2006; Mizrahi et al., 2001; Santin and Schulz, 2019; Thoby-Brisson and Simmers, 2002; Turrigiano et al., 1994; Turrigiano et al., 1995; Viteri and Schulz, 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Neurons homeostatically regulate channel voltage dependence to stabilize their activity.
source: Experimental studies have shown that neurons homeostatically regulate both channel number (Desai et al., 1999; Haedo and Golowasch, 2006; Mizrahi et al., 2001; Santin and Schulz, 2019; Thoby-Brisson and Simmers, 2002; Turrigiano et al., 1994; Turrigiano et al., 1995; Viteri and Schulz, 2023) and channel voltage dependence (Gasselin et al., 2015; Haedo and Golowasch, 2006; Thoby-Brisson and Simmers, 2002) to stabilize their activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Most computational modeling work on homeostatic mechanisms has focused on changes in channel number.
source: These mechanisms have been widely studied through computational modeling, but most of this work has focused on changes in channel number (Abbott and LeMasson, 1993; Alonso et al., 2023; Golowasch et al., 1999; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2020; LeMasson et al., 1993; O'Leary et al., 2014; Siegel et al., 1994; Srikanth and Narayanan, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple computational modeling studies.

claim: Inter-neuronal variability in activation and inactivation curves can obscure clear patterns of activity-mediated modifications when analyzed at the population level.
source: Inter-neuronal variability in activation and inactivation curves can obscure clear patterns of activity-mediated modifications, especially when analyzed at the population level (Turrigiano et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Turrigiano et al., 1995.

claim: Neurons modulate voltage dependence through rapid post-translational modifications.
source: Neurons modulate voltage dependence through mechanisms ranging from rapid post-translational modifications (Fraser and Scott, 1999; Johnson et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fraser and Scott, 1999 and Johnson et al., 1994.

claim: Neurons modulate voltage dependence through slower processes like subunit synthesis and degradation.
source: Neurons modulate voltage dependence through mechanisms ranging from rapid post-translational modifications (Fraser and Scott, 1999; Johnson et al., 1994) or slower processes like subunit synthesis and degradation (Wu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2023.

claim: Voltage dependence modulation processes are associated with calcium-mediated second messengers.
source: These processes are known to be associated with calcium-mediated second messengers.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Intracellular calcium plays an important role in maintaining neuronal activity set points.
source: Intracellular calcium is also thought to play an important role in maintaining neuronal activity set points (LeMasson et al., 1993; Turrigiano et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to LeMasson et al., 1993 and Turrigiano et al., 1994.

claim: The computational model is a single compartment, Hodgkin-Huxley type conductance-based neuron with seven intrinsic currents.
source: This model was built around a single compartment, Hodgkin–Huxley type conductance-based neuron with seven intrinsic currents (see Turrigiano et al., 1995 or Appendix 1, Neuron model).
evidence: This describes the model structure used in the study.

claim: The neuron model consists of a fast Na+ current, two Ca2+ currents, three K+ currents, a hyperpolarization-activated inward current (IH), and a leak current.
source: The neuron model consisted of a fast Na+ current, two Ca2+ currents, three K+ currents, a hyperpolarization-activated inward current (IH), and a leak current.
evidence: This describes the specific currents included in the model.

claim: The activity-dependent regulation of channel number and (in)activation curves uses intracellular Ca2+ concentrations as a proxy for the neuron's activity.
source: The activity-dependent regulation of channel number and (in)activation curves employed a strategy that uses intracellular Ca2+ concentrations as a proxy for the neuron's activity (Abbott and LeMasson, 1993; Alonso et al., 2023; Golowasch et al., 1999; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2020; LeMasson et al., 1993; O'Leary et al., 2014; Siegel et al., 1994; Srikanth and Narayanan, 2015).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model approach, supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: The model uses three Ca2+ sensors to better differentiate between the activity of tonic spiking and bursting neurons.
source: The three sensors were employed to better differentiate between the activity of tonic spiking and bursting neurons (Alonso et al., 2023; Liu et al., 1998).
evidence: This describes a feature of the model, supported by citations.

claim: The model successfully assembled a burster from random starting parameters (SP1) when both channel density and voltage dependence mechanisms were active.
source: From a set of starting randomly chosen parameters (maximal conductances and half-(in)activations), referred to as Starting Parameters 1 (SP1), the activity-dependent regulation mechanism altered the ion channel density and voltage dependences to assemble an electrical activity pattern that satisfied the Ca2+ targets.
evidence: This is a result from the simulation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: When activity-dependent regulation of maximal conductances is turned off, the model failed to assemble SP1 into a burster.
source: When activity-dependent regulation of the maximal conductances is turned off, the model failed to assemble SP1 into a burster (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation shown in Figure 1B.

claim: When the model was initialized with different starting parameters, it produced bursters with different final intrinsic properties.
source: In general, when the model was initialized with different starting parameters, it produced bursters with different final intrinsic properties.
evidence: This is a general observation from the simulations, supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Twenty degenerate bursters (SP1–SP20) were selected from over 100 bursters produced with different starting parameters.
source: Twenty degenerate bursters (SP1–SP20), conforming to standards specified in Methods, were selected from over 100 bursters produced with different starting parameters.
evidence: This describes the selection process for the models analyzed in the study.

claim: Alterations in the timescale of half-(in)activation alterations significantly impacted the period of the bursting population.
source: Figure 3A shows that alterations in the timescale of half-(in)activation alterations significantly impacted the period, interburst interval, spike height, and maximum hyperpolarization of the entire bursting population.
evidence: This is a result shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: Alterations in the timescale of half-(in)activation alterations significantly impacted the interburst interval of the bursting population.
source: Figure 3A shows that alterations in the timescale of half-(in)activation alterations significantly impacted the period, interburst interval, spike height, and maximum hyperpolarization of the entire bursting population.
evidence: This is a result shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: Alterations in the timescale of half-(in)activation alterations significantly impacted the spike height of the bursting population.
source: Figure 3A shows that alterations in the timescale of half-(in)activation alterations significantly impacted the period, interburst interval, spike height, and maximum hyperpolarization of the entire bursting population.
evidence: This is a result shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: Alterations in the timescale of half-(in)activation alterations significantly impacted the maximum hyperpolarization of the bursting population.
source: Figure 3A shows that alterations in the timescale of half-(in)activation alterations significantly impacted the period, interburst interval, spike height, and maximum hyperpolarization of the entire bursting population.
evidence: This is a result shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: Both bursters assembled with fast and infinitely slow half-(in)activation alterations appeared to terminate using the same mechanism: hyperpolarization via the calcium-activated potassium current.
source: In both cases, the resulting burster appeared to terminate using the same mechanism: hyperpolarization via the calcium-activated potassium current.
evidence: This is an observation from the currentscape analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The burster constructed without half-(in)activation alterations possessed a higher maximal conductance for IKCa than the burster constructed with half-(in)activation alterations.
source: Note that the burster constructed without half-(in)activation alterations possessed a higher maximal conductance for IKCa than the burster constructed with half-(in)activation alterations (Figure 3C, mauve dot).
evidence: This is a specific observation from Figure 3C comparing two conditions.

claim: The burster constructed with half-(in)activation alterations had more depolarized half-(in)activations for IKCa than the burster constructed without half-(in)activation alterations.
source: Moreover, the latter burster had more depolarized half-(in)activations (Figure 3C, mauve dot).
evidence: This is a specific observation from Figure 3C comparing two conditions.

claim: The observation that bursters without half-(in)activation alterations have higher IKCa maximal conductance and more hyperpolarized half-activations held true for SP2–SP20 as well.
source: In fact, this observation held true for SP2–SP20 as well (Figure 3C).
evidence: This extends the observation to the full set of models, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When half-(in)activations are fast, the time evolution of α shows an abrupt jump as it searches for a voltage-dependence configuration that meets calcium targets.
source: When half-(in)activations are fast, the time evolution of α—which tracks how far the activity pattern is from its targets (see Methods)—shows an abrupt jump as it searches for a voltage-dependence configuration that meets calcium targets (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Slowing the half-(in)activations alterations reduces the abrupt fluctuations in α.
source: Slowing the half-(in)activations alterations reduces these abrupt fluctuations (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Different timescales of half-(in)activation alteration led the model through different paths in the space of activity profiles and intrinsic properties.
source: Because each timescale of half-(in)activation produces a different channel repertoire at each time step, different timescales of half-(in)activation alteration led the model through a different path in the space of activity profiles and intrinsic properties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Different timescales of half-(in)activation regulation resulted in distinct final activity patterns, all of which were consistent with the Ca2+ targets.
source: Ultimately, this resulted in distinct final activity patterns, all of which were consistent with the Ca2+ targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The model simulates an increase in extracellular potassium concentration by altering both the potassium reversal potential and the leak reversal potential.
source: In particular, we modeled an increase in extracellular potassium concentration by altering both the potassium reversal potential and the leak reversal potential (see Methods).
evidence: This describes the perturbation protocol used in the recovery simulations.

claim: The perturbation caused all 20 models to experience depolarization block.
source: However, once extracellular potassium concentration increases, the shifts in reversal potentials cause all 20 models to experience depolarization block.
evidence: This is a result from the perturbation simulations.

claim: Although all three recovery conditions eventually re-stabilized to activity patterns that satisfied the calcium targets, the resulting burst patterns were different.
source: Notably, although all three cases eventually re-stabilized to activity patterns that satisfied the calcium targets, the resulting burst patterns were different.
evidence: This is an observation from the recovery simulations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SP1 was one of eleven models that successfully recovered under all three homeostatic conditions.
source: SP1 was one of eleven models that successfully recovered under all three homeostatic conditions.
evidence: This is a specific result from the recovery simulations.

claim: Eight models required some form of half-(in)activation modulation to stabilize after perturbation.
source: Eight models required some form of half-(in)activation modulation to stabilize; in these cases, conductance regulation alone was not sufficient for recovery.
evidence: This is a result from the recovery simulations.

claim: Two models only recovered when half-(in)activation changes were fast.
source: Among these eight, two only recovered when half-(in)activation changes were fast, and another two only recovered when they were slow.
evidence: This is a specific result from the recovery simulations.

claim: Two models only recovered when half-(in)activation changes were slow.
source: Among these eight, two only recovered when half-(in)activation changes were fast, and another two only recovered when they were slow.
evidence: This is a specific result from the recovery simulations.

claim: For some models, the ability to recover bursting activity depended on both the presence and speed of half-(in)activation modulation.
source: Evidently, for some models, the ability to recover bursting activity depended on both the presence and speed of half-(in)activation modulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recovery simulation results.

claim: The half-activation voltage of the KCa current differs significantly between fast and intermediate timescales of half-(in)activation regulation after recovery.
source: Similarly, the half-activation voltage of the KCa current differs significantly between these two timescales (Figure 5C), paralleling the differences observed in Figure 3C.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the recovery simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In models that successfully recovered from perturbation, the timescale of voltage-dependence modulation influenced both the resulting activity patterns and the intrinsic parameters of the stabilized bursters.
source: In models that successfully recovered from perturbation, the timescale of voltage-dependence modulation influenced both the resulting activity patterns and the intrinsic parameters of the stabilized bursters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recovery simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: While all models met the activity target regardless of whether voltage-dependence modulation was present, recovery after perturbation depended on both the presence and timescale of this mechanism.
source: While all models met the activity target regardless of whether voltage-dependence modulation was present, recovery after perturbation depended on both the presence and timescale of this mechanism.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the study.

claim: The timescale of half-(in)activation modulation shaped the stabilized neuron's specific activity characteristics and underlying intrinsic parameters in both initial assembly and recovery scenarios.
source: Furthermore, in both scenarios, the timescale shaped the stabilized neuron's specific activity characteristics and underlying intrinsic parameters.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the study.

claim: The timescale of half-(in)activation modulation plays a general role in sculpting stable activity states.
source: This suggests a general role for the timescale of half-(in)activation modulation in sculpting stable activity states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Fast timescale post-translational alterations can be implemented by second messengers that are anchored next to ion channels.
source: Fast timescale post-translational alterations can be implemented by second messengers that are anchored next to ion channels (Fraser and Scott, 1999; Johnson et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fraser and Scott, 1999 and Johnson et al., 1994.

claim: Fast timescale post-translational alterations can be implemented by second messengers that diffuse across the cytosol.
source: Fast timescale post-translational alterations can be implemented by second messengers that are anchored next to ion channels (Fraser and Scott, 1999; Johnson et al., 1994) or second messengers that diffuse across the cytosol (Agarwal et al., 2016; Zaccolo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Agarwal et al., 2016 and Zaccolo et al., 2006.

claim: Phosphorylation by kinases is a commonly studied post-translational modification.
source: Phosphorylation by kinases is a commonly studied post-translational modification; however, there are other modifications that also occur on these timescales, such as S-nitrosylation (Broillet, 1999).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge with a citation to Broillet, 1999 for S-nitrosylation.

claim: S-nitrosylation is a post-translational modification that occurs on fast timescales.
source: Phosphorylation by kinases is a commonly studied post-translational modification; however, there are other modifications that also occur on these timescales, such as S-nitrosylation (Broillet, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Broillet, 1999.

claim: Neurons can modulate the transcription and translation of auxiliary subunits based on intracellular calcium levels on slower timescales.
source: On slower timescales, the neuron can modulate the transcription and translation of auxiliary subunits based on intracellular calcium levels.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Potassium Channel-Interacting Proteins are controlled by CREB.
source: For instance, Potassium Channel-Interacting Proteins are known to be controlled by CREB (Wu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2023.

claim: Developmental phases are marked by changes in ion channel density and voltage dependence, leading to distinct electrical activity at each stage.
source: Indeed, developmental phases are marked by changes in ion channel density and voltage dependence, leading to distinct electrical activity at each stage (Baccaglini and Spitzer, 1977; Gao and Ziskind-Conhaim, 1998; Goldberg et al., 2011; Hunsberger and Mynlieff, 2020; McCormick and Prince, 1987; Moody and Bosma, 2005; O'Leary et al., 2014; Picken Bahrey and Moody, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to developmental studies.

claim: Impairments in a neuron's ability to modulate the voltage dependence of its channels may lead to disruptions in activity-dependent homeostasis.
source: These observations all suggest that impairments in a neuron's ability to modulate the voltage dependence of its channels may lead to disruptions in activity-dependent homeostasis.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Disruptions in homeostatic processes are thought to contribute to the pathogenesis of addiction.
source: This may have implications for conditions such as addiction (Kourrich et al., 2015) and Alzheimer's disease (Styr and Slutsky, 2018), where disruptions in homeostatic processes are thought to contribute to pathogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kourrich et al., 2015.

claim: Disruptions in homeostatic processes are thought to contribute to the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease.
source: This may have implications for conditions such as addiction (Kourrich et al., 2015) and Alzheimer's disease (Styr and Slutsky, 2018), where disruptions in homeostatic processes are thought to contribute to pathogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Styr and Slutsky, 2018.

claim: When a neuron begins from a state of no activity and small randomly specified channel densities, changes in channel density are essential for attaining activity.
source: In conclusion, our findings suggest that when a neuron begins from a state of no activity and small randomly specified channel densities, changes in channel density are essential for attaining activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results, particularly Figure 1B.

claim: Activity-dependent changes in channel voltage dependence alone did not assemble bursting from low-conductance initial states.
source: In this context, activity-dependent changes in channel voltage dependence alone did not assemble bursting from these low-conductance initial states (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Fast shifts in half-(in)activation constrain the types of activity characteristics and intrinsic properties a neuron ultimately expresses.
source: However, our results demonstrate that fast shifts in half-(in)activation constrain the types of activity characteristics and intrinsic properties a neuron ultimately expresses (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Fast alterations in half-(in)activation, while subtle, manifest over long timescales required to assemble activity.
source: These fast alterations, while subtle, manifest over long timescales required to assemble activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: This study exemplifies how interactions between processes operating on different timescales can influence one another.
source: This study exemplifies how interactions between processes operating on different timescales can influence one another.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the implications of the study.

claim: The neuron's capacitance (C) was set to 1 nF.
source: The neuron's capacitance (C) was set to 1 nF.
evidence: This is a specific parameter value used in the model.

claim: The equilibrium/reversal potentials of the sodium current, hyperpolarization-activated cation current, potassium currents, and leak current were +30, –20, –80, and –50 mV, respectively.
source: The equilibrium/reversal potentials of the sodium current, hyperpolarization-activated cation current, potassium currents, and leak current were +30, –20, –80, and –50 mV, respectively.
evidence: These are specific parameter values used in the model.

claim: The calcium equilibrium potential was computed via the Nernst equation using the computed internal Ca2+ concentration and an external Ca2+ concentration of 3 mM at a temperature of 10°C.
source: The calcium equilibrium potential was computed via the Nernst equation (Equation A5) using the computed internal Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i) and an external Ca2+ concentration of 3 mM (temperature was 10°C).
evidence: This describes how a specific parameter was calculated in the model.

claim: A 2.5-fold increase in extracellular potassium concentration corresponds to a change in the potassium reversal potential from −80 to −55 mV using the Nernst equation.
source: Using the Nernst equation, this shift corresponds to a change in the potassium reversal potential from −80 to −55 mV.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the Nernst equation for the perturbation protocol.

claim: The perturbation impacts the leak reversal potential because leak current in the model includes a potassium component.
source: We assume that leak current in our model includes a potassium component, so that the perturbation also impacts the leak reversal potential.
evidence: This is an assumption made in the model for the perturbation protocol.

claim: The new leak reversal potential after perturbation was calculated to be approximately –32 mV.
source: The new leak reversal potential was calculated using standard computation involving the conductance-weighted average of potassium and sodium reversal potentials, yielding a value of approximately –32 mV.
evidence: This is a calculated value for the perturbation protocol.

claim: The leak maximal conductance for the model is fixed at 0.01 μS.
source: The leak maximal conductance for our model is fixed at 0.01 μS.
evidence: This is a specific parameter value used in the model.

claim: The model was integrated using the Tsitouras 5 implementation of Runga–Kutta 4 (5) in Julia's DifferentialEquations.jl package.
source: The model was integrated using the Tsitouras 5 implementation of Runga–Kutta 4 (5) in Julia's DifferentialEquations.jl package (Tsitouras, 2011).
evidence: This describes the numerical integration method used, with a citation to Tsitouras, 2011.

claim: The simulation was saved every 0.5 ms regardless of step size.
source: The simulation was saved every 0.5 ms regardless of step size (step size of the integrator was adaptive and left unspecified).
evidence: This describes a technical detail of the simulation implementation.

claim: The maximum number of iterations for the integrator was set to 10^10 and relative tolerance was set to 0.0001.
source: The maximum number of iterations was set to 1010 and relative tolerance was set to 0.0001.
evidence: These are specific parameter values used in the numerical integration.

claim: Regular bursters are defined as activity patterns that exhibited groups of spikes separated by regular quiescent gaps in activity.
source: We defined regular bursters as activity patterns that exhibited groups of spikes separated by regular quiescent gaps in activity.
evidence: This is a definition used in the study.

claim: The model assembled bursters from over 95% of the randomly chosen starting parameters using the selected calcium targets.
source: 'Consistently', in this context, meant that the model assembled bursters from over 95% of the randomly chosen starting parameters.
evidence: This is a result describing the success rate of the model.

claim: A total of 111 regular bursters were assembled from a wide range of randomly initialized starting parameters.
source: Using the obtained calcium targets, we assembled a total of 111 regular bursters from a wide range of randomly initialized starting parameters.
evidence: This describes the initial pool of models generated.

claim: The 111 models were filtered by slow wave amplitude, retaining only those with amplitudes less than 25 mV, reducing the pool to 80 models.
source: We first filtered the 111 models by slow wave amplitude, retaining only those with amplitudes less than 25 mV. This excluded models with unusually large oscillations and preserved activity patterns with waveforms similar to those shown in Figure 7C, reducing the pool to 80 models.
evidence: This describes a selection step in the analysis.

claim: The peak of the period distribution for the 80 filtered models is between 380 and 500 ms.
source: The peak of this distribution is between 380 and 500 ms.
evidence: This is an observation from the period distribution shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The model assumes a single, uniform time constant for modifying all intrinsic currents.
source: First, the model assumes a single, uniform time constant for modifying all intrinsic currents.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model discussed in the Methods section.

claim: The framework assumes post-translational modifications are removed as quickly (or slowly) as they are added.
source: Second, our framework assumes post-translational modifications are removed as quickly (or slowly) as they are added.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model discussed in the Methods section.

claim: CaMKII undergoes autophosphorylation, enabling a brief calcium signal to induce long-lasting changes in protein activity.
source: For instance, the calcium-mediated second messenger CaMKII undergoes autophosphorylation, enabling a brief calcium signal to induce long-lasting changes in protein activity (Hudmon and Schulman, 2002; Kennedy, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hudmon and Schulman, 2002 and Kennedy, 1989.

claim: CaMKII autophosphorylation is known to influence intrinsic excitability of neurons.
source: This autophosphorylation is known to influence intrinsic excitability of neurons (Sametsky et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sametsky et al., 2009.

claim: CaMKII autophosphorylation may modulate the voltage-dependence of CaV2 channels.
source: This autophosphorylation is known to influence intrinsic excitability of neurons (Sametsky et al., 2009) and may modulate the voltage-dependence of CaV2 channels (Jiang et al., 2008), which putatively contribute to ICaS.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2008.

claim: cAMP can shift the half-activation of IH, and this effect saturates at high cAMP concentrations.
source: For example, while cAMP can shift the half-activation of IH, this effect saturates at high cAMP concentrations (DiFrancesco and Tortora, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to DiFrancesco and Tortora, 1991.

claim: Activity-dependent shifts in voltage-dependent time constants have been observed without concomitant shifts in activation curves.
source: For instance, activity-dependent shifts in voltage-dependent time constants have been observed without concomitant shifts in activation curves (Thoby-Brisson and Simmers, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thoby-Brisson and Simmers, 2002.

claim: With certain calcium-activated potassium currents, the center and slope of the activation curve depend on calcium concentration.
source: Nonetheless, with certain calcium-activated potassium currents, the center and slope of the activation curve depend on calcium concentration (Wang and Brenner, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang and Brenner, 2006.

claim: Cells can detect the temporal patterns and specific pathways of calcium entry, leading to specific activity-dependent changes.
source: Nonetheless, the extent to which this crosstalk occurs is not known, although it is known that cells can detect the temporal patterns and specific pathways of calcium entry, leading to specific activity-dependent changes (Bito et al., 1997; Fields et al., 1997; Gallin and Greenberg, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bito et al., 1997; Fields et al., 1997; and Gallin and Greenberg, 1995.

claim: Neurons coregulate IA and IH expression, so that a change in one current is associated with a change in the other.
source: For example, neurons coregulate IA and IH expression, so that a change in one current is associated with a change in the other (MacLean et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to MacLean et al., 2005.

claim: A neuromodulatory environment may play a role in coordinating ion channel levels.
source: A neuromodulatory environment may also play a role in coordinating ion channel levels (Khorkova and Golowasch, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Khorkova and Golowasch, 2007.
